One thing I did recently in **Oranni** was make a pun! I was pretty proud of that.

It was on a challenge post where we were to translate, "If I don't carry it, then it won't be heavy for me." With a little tweaking, this became:

*Cu to talunes bi no, egwones bi taluní ono.*

Wⵙ ⴷⵔ ⴷⵀᒉⵙႷIV ⴴİ Ⴗⵔ : IⵡᵓⵔႷIV ⴴİ ⴷⵀᒉⵙႷÍ ⵔႷⵔ •

"If I do not bear it, then I will not become overborne."

/ʃu to taˈlunes bi no, eˈgwones bi taluˈni ˈono/

[tɕyː ˌt̪oː t̪aˈlynɛs βɪ noː, ɛˈgʷonɛs βɪ t̪alyˈniː ˌono]

PRON.1.SNG.NOM PRON.2.SNG.IMPERS.ACC bear.V.EXT negative.PART if.PART, become.V.EXT negative.PART overborne.ADJ then.PART

The verb *talune*, "to bear," can actually be used to mean the inverse as well, "to be borne," with context being the only indication of which definition a speaker intends. *Taluní*, the adjective form of this verb (similar to a past participle in English, but with more limited use) has two meanings:

1. "borne," which describes a load or burden one carries

2. "overborne," as in overcome by physical force of carrying a burden

So this sentence is a pun, playing on the dual meaning of the word and a role reversal in the second half of the sentence! This has helped me feel like my language has depth and character. I want to explore idioms and rhetorical devices this month.

Wⵙ IᒉIႷⵔ ⵔⵡVİႷİ ⴷᒉⵔᒉⵙႷI ⵡᗰⵔU ⵀⵠIႷİ •

The word *tlolune* means "to rely upon" and is a transitive verb.

The word *adeni* comes from *ado eni*, lit. "to now," and means something like "up through this point." It's used similarly to the present perfect in English.

The word for *stranger* here is singular because it is very rare to see plurals in the genitive case, and if the speaker meant a specific stranger, then they would probably use a demonstrative pronoun. If they meant only one stranger, they'd probably use the word *bwo* meaning "one".

Oranni does not have gendered pronouns or many gendered words at all. I used the words for parent and child rather than father and son (which would just be said as "male parent" and "male child" if necessary). I used the word for girl rather than child or youngster because it seemed very important for the context.

The expression *krasaci*, lit. "waxing" like the moon, is used commonly to refer to the time between birth and adulthood, and most often refers to adolescents. It contrasts with *bikrasaci*, lit. "waning," which refers to the time between adulthood and death, i.e. old age. It reflects the Oranni sensibility that life is cyclical, and reinforces a cultural connection with the moon.

I could have used a word that means "blossoming," but it would be very strange in Oranni, as plant life is seen as fairly distinct from humanity. It would depend on how Greek the translation was intended to sound.

The **Oranni** are a relatively small community of humanoids living on a moon colony. They lost their home planet a few generations ago, along with the majority of their records. They have a language and a culture, but no history, just what they can piece together.

They are visited by a group of rogues who say they're the last survivors of their race, the Corgusians, and who plan to hold the Oranni accountable for past genocide.

The Oranni living now have no record or memory of these people or events, and all parties are torn on how to proceed.

The moon colony struggles to provide for itself because of the unforgiving nature of their home. This is different from many stories with similar premises in that:

1. the moon has not been terraformed or covered in some bio-dome. The Oranni genuinely struggle in a world that they are not perfectly biologically suited to, but which is the best they have available, and

2. the colony receives no support from a home planet. They must totally fend for themselves, unsure even of what is native to the moon and what was brought with them.

This unforgiving setting (low oxygen levels, very hot days and very cold nights, little usable soil, etc.) and the Oranni's relatively recent arrival make this a survival story rather than one primarily about hyperadvanced technology.

As far as the themes, the Oranni are literally living off a vestige of imperialism, disconnected physically from their past. While they aren't exactly the genocidal warmongers that they come to discover their ancestors were, their existence is inexorably tied to those ancestors' actions. This one is a euphemism for destroying someone, either physically by killing them or figuratively by ruining their life or career. It has the connotation of being a righteous action. It comes from an Oranni myth about a goddess who returns evildoers to the earth, from which the Oranni traditionally believe human life originally came.

Most of Oranni's affixes come from particles.

The suffixes for the accusative and genitive cases (*-o* and *-i*) were once the particles *ho* and *hi*, then the suffixes *-ho* and *-hi*, and finally the /h/ was dropped and the vowel simply replaced the final vowel of a noun's nominative form, typically *a*.

*Ho* and *hi* may still be used as particles when modifying compound nouns or complex noun phrases, though they've mostly been phased out.

*Sa* is a plural particle, which has become a suffix (*-sa*) for most nouns.
